title.en: From fibre to thread: spinning and natural and synthetic fibres

text.en: Pull a strand of cotton and twist it slowly. It becomes stronger as you spin it. Wind it onto a pencil.

Twisting cotton fibres together to make thread or yarn is called spinning. A charkha, or spinning wheel, does it just as the pencil did. The thin hair-like piece you get on untwisting is a fibre.
Gandhi ji showed the importance of being self-sufficient. Making your own cloth by spinning cotton and weaving it was a symbol of the freedom struggle and of being atmanirbhar. This cloth is called khadi.
India was the first country to cultivate and use cotton for clothes.
Natural fibres come from cotton, bamboo, linen, wool and silk. Silk comes from the cocoon of the silk moth: cocoons are put in hot water and the thread is gently pulled out.
Silkworm life cycle: eggs, caterpillar, cocoon, moth. A life cycle is the pattern of growth and change every living thing goes through.
Synthetic fibres such as nylon, polyester, terylene and rayon are made by humans from artificial materials. We use both natural and synthetic fibres.
India is the largest producer of jute in the world.
Activity: look at your clothes and bags and list whether they are natural or synthetic and what you like about them.

text.en: Cotton, silk and wool are natural.
Nylon and polyester are synthetic.
Both kinds are used in clothes.

points.en: Natural fibres come from plants and animals.
